characterized_levers.name: PSG Escalation Threshold
characterized_levers.consequences: Lowering the threshold for escalating to full PSG increases data richness and confidence in event characterization, but also raises technician workload, participant burden, and scoring costs. Conversely, a higher threshold reduces burden but risks missing subtle or atypical events, potentially skewing the phenotyping analysis and undermining the event-triage tool development.
options: Require two independent technician flags within a single night before escalating to full PSG, ensuring high confidence in potential events but potentially missing subtle or brief episodes
Escalate to full PSG upon any single technician flag, maximizing event capture at the cost of increased technician workload and participant burden from more frequent hookups
Implement an automated pre-screening algorithm using dry-electrode EEG data to identify potential events, escalating to full PSG only when the algorithm and a technician both flag an episode
characterized_levers.review: Balancing PSG escalation thresholds involves a trade-off between data richness and operational burden, impacting both phenotyping accuracy and resource allocation.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: The PSG escalation threshold impacts data richness and workload, but doesn't fundamentally alter the project's success. It's a tactical decision within the broader data acquisition strategy.
characterized_levers.description: The PSG Escalation Threshold determines when full polysomnography is deployed, balancing data richness with resource constraints. A lower threshold captures more events but increases workload and costs. Success is measured by the number of adjudicated events captured and the accuracy of phenotyping, weighed against technician burden and budget adherence. This directly impacts the study's ability to characterize parasomnia patterns.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever works in synergy with Physiological Monitoring Density; more dense monitoring can inform the escalation decision. It also amplifies Annotation Granularity, as richer PSG data enables more detailed annotation.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Protocol Deviation Tolerance. A lower threshold may lead to more deviations as technicians react to potential events, while a higher threshold might miss important deviations.

characterized_levers.name: Participant Inclusion Criteria
characterized_levers.consequences: Relaxing inclusion criteria broadens the recruitment pool and accelerates enrollment, but increases the risk of admitting participants with comorbid conditions or atypical parasomnias, potentially diluting the homogeneity of the study population and complicating data interpretation. Conversely, stricter criteria improve data quality but slow recruitment and may introduce selection bias, limiting the generalizability of findings.
options: Include participants with well-controlled comorbid sleep disorders such as mild restless legs syndrome or treated sleep apnea, accepting potential confounding factors in exchange for faster enrollment
Enforce strict exclusion criteria, excluding any participant with a history of comorbid sleep disorders, ensuring a homogenous sample but potentially prolonging recruitment timelines
Stratify participants by comorbidity status and conduct subgroup analyses to account for potential confounding effects, balancing recruitment speed with data quality and analytical rigor
characterized_levers.review: Inclusion criteria stringency affects the trade-off between recruitment speed and data homogeneity, influencing both statistical power and the generalizability of findings.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Participant inclusion criteria directly affect the study population and the generalizability of findings. Poor criteria could lead to a skewed sample and invalidate the results.
characterized_levers.description: Participant Inclusion Criteria define the target population, balancing recruitment speed with data homogeneity. Stricter criteria improve data quality but slow enrollment. Success is measured by recruitment rate, sample representativeness, and the statistical power to detect meaningful differences. This lever shapes the generalizability of the study's findings.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Control Group Composition. Tighter inclusion criteria necessitate a more carefully matched control group to ensure valid comparisons and reduce confounding.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Recruitment Channel Mix. Relaxing inclusion criteria may allow for greater reliance on the sleep clinic, while stricter criteria require broader outreach.

characterized_levers.name: Recruitment Channel Mix
characterized_levers.consequences: Over-reliance on the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic provides a readily accessible patient pool but may introduce referral bias, skewing the sample towards more severe or treatment-seeking cases. Expanding recruitment to regional neurologists and the DGS network broadens the reach but requires more outreach effort and may yield a lower conversion rate. A pharmaceutical partnership could accelerate recruitment but introduces potential conflicts of interest.
options: Prioritize recruitment through the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic to leverage existing infrastructure and patient flow, accepting potential referral bias as a limitation
Actively cultivate relationships with regional neurologists and the DGS network to diversify the recruitment pool, investing in outreach and education to increase referrals
Secure a pharmaceutical industry partnership to leverage their patient network and marketing resources, accepting a 30-day pre-publication comment window as a condition
characterized_levers.review: Recruitment channel selection balances access to participants with the risk of referral bias, impacting sample representativeness and external validity.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Recruitment channels influence the speed and representativeness of enrollment, but are not a core strategic decision gating the project's success.
characterized_levers.description: Recruitment Channel Mix determines how participants are sourced, balancing access with potential bias. Prioritizing the sleep clinic offers convenience but may skew the sample. Success is measured by recruitment rate, sample representativeness, and the cost-effectiveness of each channel. This lever influences the external validity of the study.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Participant Inclusion Criteria. Broader recruitment channels are needed to support stricter inclusion criteria and achieve target enrollment numbers.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with the Data Security Protocol. Expanding recruitment channels may require additional measures to ensure data privacy and compliance with ethical guidelines.

characterized_levers.name: Event-Triage Automation Level
characterized_levers.consequences: Investing heavily in sophisticated event-triage algorithms reduces manual review burden and accelerates annotation throughput, but requires substantial computational resources and may introduce algorithmic bias, potentially missing subtle or atypical events. Conversely, relying primarily on manual review ensures high accuracy but limits throughput and scalability, potentially delaying publication and grant submission.
options: Develop a highly sensitive event-triage algorithm that prioritizes recall over precision, minimizing missed events at the cost of increased false positives and manual review of non-events
Focus on a highly specific event-triage algorithm that prioritizes precision over recall, minimizing false positives at the cost of potentially missing subtle or atypical events
Implement a hybrid approach combining a moderately sensitive algorithm with a technician-in-the-loop review process, balancing automation with human oversight to optimize accuracy and throughput
characterized_levers.review: The level of event-triage automation involves a trade-off between annotation throughput and event detection accuracy, impacting both efficiency and data quality.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: The level of event-triage automation directly impacts the feasibility of analyzing the data and achieving Aim 3. Insufficient automation could cripple the project.
characterized_levers.description: Event-Triage Automation Level determines the degree to which algorithms assist in identifying parasomnia events, balancing throughput with accuracy. Higher automation reduces manual review but risks bias. Success is measured by annotation throughput, algorithm performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity), and agreement with human scorers. This lever impacts efficiency and data quality.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Annotation Granularity. Efficient event triage allows for more detailed annotation of identified events, enhancing the richness of the dataset.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Inter-Rater Reliability Threshold. Higher automation may reduce the need for extensive inter-rater reliability checks, but also risks introducing systematic biases.

characterized_levers.name: Environmental Modification Intensity
characterized_levers.consequences: Extensive environmental modifications, such as padded walls and restricted-opening windows, minimize participant injury risk but may create an artificial environment that suppresses naturalistic behavior, reducing the ecological validity of the data. Conversely, minimal modifications preserve a domestic feel but increase the potential for injury, raising ethical concerns and potentially deterring recruitment.
options: Implement extensive environmental modifications to minimize participant injury risk, prioritizing safety over ecological validity and potentially suppressing naturalistic behavior
Maintain a minimally modified domestic environment to preserve ecological validity, accepting a higher level of potential injury risk and implementing enhanced monitoring protocols
Adopt a tiered approach, implementing targeted modifications based on individual participant risk profiles, balancing safety with ecological validity and personalized care
characterized_levers.review: Environmental modification intensity balances participant safety with ecological validity, influencing both ethical considerations and the naturalness of observed behavior.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Environmental modification intensity is a primary lever because it directly impacts participant safety and the ecological validity of the data, influencing ethical considerations and data quality.
characterized_levers.description: Environmental Modification Intensity dictates the extent to which the residential facility is altered for safety, balancing participant well-being with ecological validity. Extensive modifications minimize injury risk but may suppress natural behavior. Success is measured by the absence of serious injuries, participant comfort, and the naturalness of observed behavior.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Nocturnal Safety Protocol Rigor. More intense environmental modifications can reduce the need for constant vigilance in safety protocols.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Residential Ambiance Design. Extensive modifications may detract from the domestic feel, making the environment feel more clinical and less natural.

characterized_levers.name: Protocol Deviation Tolerance
characterized_levers.consequences: Strict adherence to the protocol ensures data consistency and reduces variability, but limits flexibility in addressing unforeseen challenges or individual participant needs, potentially hindering recruitment and data collection. Conversely, allowing for protocol deviations increases flexibility but introduces variability and complicates data analysis, potentially undermining the rigor of the study.
options: Enforce strict adherence to the protocol, minimizing variability and ensuring data consistency at the cost of reduced flexibility in addressing individual participant needs
Allow for protocol deviations on a case-by-case basis with PI approval, increasing flexibility but introducing variability and requiring careful documentation and justification
Develop pre-defined protocol modification pathways for common scenarios, balancing standardization with adaptability and ensuring consistent decision-making
characterized_levers.review: Protocol deviation tolerance balances data consistency with operational flexibility, impacting both rigor and the ability to adapt to unforeseen circumstances.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Protocol deviation tolerance affects data consistency and flexibility, but is a procedural matter rather than a core strategic choice.
characterized_levers.description: Protocol Deviation Tolerance defines the acceptable range of variation from the standard research procedures. High tolerance allows for adapting to individual participant needs or unforeseen circumstances, potentially improving recruitment and retention. Key metrics include the number and type of deviations, their documented justification, and their impact on data quality and analysis.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Stay-Extension Protocol, as flexibility in the core protocol may necessitate or justify extending a participant's stay to gather sufficient data despite initial deviations.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Inter-Rater Reliability Threshold, as increased protocol deviations can introduce variability that makes it more difficult to achieve high agreement between independent scorers.

characterized_levers.name: Residential Ambiance Design
characterized_levers.consequences: A more clinical environment may improve data quality by reducing extraneous movements and artifacts, but it could also suppress naturalistic parasomnia events. A homelike setting might increase event frequency but introduce more noise and require more intensive cleaning and maintenance.
options: Prioritize a highly controlled, standardized environment with minimal personal items to reduce variability and potential hazards
Create a deliberately 'lived-in' aesthetic with comfortable furnishings and personalized touches to encourage naturalistic sleep behaviors
Implement a modular design allowing for rapid reconfiguration between clinical and homelike states to assess environmental influence
characterized_levers.review: Balancing clinical control with naturalistic observation is key, as a sterile environment may inhibit parasomnia events, while a chaotic one complicates data analysis.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Residential ambiance design influences participant comfort and data quality, but is not a top-level strategic decision. It's a design choice within the facility setup.
characterized_levers.description: Residential Ambiance Design determines the physical environment of the sleep suites, balancing clinical control with a comfortable, naturalistic setting. Success is measured by participant comfort and reported sleep quality, alongside the frequency and naturalness of captured parasomnia events. The goal is to minimize environmental influence on sleep behavior.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Recruitment Channel Mix. A more comfortable, less clinical environment may broaden the appeal of the study and improve recruitment rates through various channels.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Nocturnal Safety Protocol Rigor. A more homelike environment may necessitate stricter safety protocols to mitigate risks associated with a less controlled setting.

characterized_levers.name: Nocturnal Safety Protocol Rigor
characterized_levers.consequences: Stricter safety protocols, such as continuous video monitoring and physical restraints, minimize participant risk but may increase anxiety and suppress parasomnia events. Looser protocols enhance ecological validity but elevate the risk of injury or property damage, potentially increasing insurance costs and ethical scrutiny.
options: Implement continuous real-time video monitoring with immediate technician intervention for any detected out-of-bed activity
Employ passive safety measures like padded walls and silent alarms, intervening only when a participant exhibits clear signs of distress or danger
Utilize a tiered safety system, escalating monitoring intensity based on individual participant risk profiles and prior event history
characterized_levers.review: Overly restrictive safety measures may inhibit natural behavior, while insufficient precautions could lead to participant injury and ethical breaches.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Nocturnal safety protocol rigor is a primary lever because it directly impacts participant safety and ethical considerations, potentially affecting recruitment and project viability.
characterized_levers.description: Nocturnal Safety Protocol Rigor dictates the measures taken to ensure participant safety during sleep monitoring. Success is measured by the absence of serious adverse events, balanced against the potential for these measures to suppress natural sleep behaviors. The goal is to minimize risk without compromising data quality.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Participant Inclusion Criteria. Stricter safety protocols may allow for the inclusion of participants with slightly higher risk profiles, expanding the potential recruitment pool.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Residential Ambiance Design. More rigorous safety protocols, such as continuous monitoring, can make the residential environment feel less homelike and more clinical.

characterized_levers.name: Enhanced-Night PSG Frequency
characterized_levers.consequences: More frequent enhanced-night PSG provides richer physiological data and facilitates more precise event characterization, but it also increases participant burden, technician workload, and data processing costs. Less frequent PSG reduces costs and burden but limits the ability to capture subtle physiological changes associated with parasomnia events.
options: Schedule enhanced-night PSG on every night of a participant's stay to maximize physiological data capture
Limit enhanced-night PSG to the first, middle, and last nights of a participant's stay to minimize burden and cost
Implement an adaptive PSG schedule, increasing frequency during periods of high event activity or suspected physiological change
characterized_levers.review: Balancing data richness with participant burden and cost is crucial, as excessive PSG can be intrusive, while infrequent PSG misses key events.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Enhanced-night PSG frequency affects data richness and participant burden, but is a tactical decision within the data acquisition strategy.
characterized_levers.description: Enhanced-Night PSG Frequency determines how often participants undergo full polysomnography during their stay. More frequent PSG yields richer data but increases participant burden and costs. Success is measured by the quality and completeness of physiological data, balanced against participant comfort and resource constraints.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Physiological Monitoring Density, as increasing the frequency of enhanced-night PSG complements the continuous low-burden monitoring to provide a comprehensive dataset.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Annotation Granularity. Increased PSG frequency generates more data, potentially requiring a trade-off with the level of detail in manual annotation to manage workload.

characterized_levers.name: Longitudinal Phenotyping Depth
characterized_levers.consequences: Deeper phenotyping, including detailed neuropsychological assessments and genetic screening, provides a more comprehensive understanding of parasomnia etiology but increases participant burden and study complexity. Shallower phenotyping reduces burden but limits the ability to identify underlying risk factors and disease mechanisms.
options: Conduct extensive neuropsychological testing, detailed sleep questionnaires, and genetic screening on all participants to identify potential biomarkers
Focus on core clinical features and basic demographic data to minimize participant burden and maintain a streamlined research protocol
Employ a staged phenotyping approach, initially collecting basic data and then selectively expanding data collection based on preliminary findings
characterized_levers.review: The depth of phenotyping must balance the desire for comprehensive data with the practical constraints of participant burden and study resources.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Longitudinal phenotyping depth influences the comprehensiveness of the data, but is not a core strategic decision. It's a scope choice within the research program.
characterized_levers.description: Longitudinal Phenotyping Depth defines the scope of data collected beyond core sleep parameters, including neuropsychological and genetic assessments. Deeper phenotyping aims to uncover underlying mechanisms but increases participant burden and study complexity. Success is measured by the richness of the dataset and its contribution to understanding parasomnia etiology.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: This lever synergizes with Control Group Composition. Deeper phenotyping in the parasomnia group necessitates a similarly detailed characterization of the control group to enable meaningful comparisons.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: This lever conflicts with Recruitment Channel Mix. More extensive phenotyping requirements may narrow the pool of eligible and willing participants, impacting recruitment strategies and potentially requiring more intensive recruitment efforts.

characterized_levers.name: Control Group Composition
characterized_levers.consequences: A larger, more diverse control group provides a more robust baseline for comparison and improves the generalizability of findings, but it also increases recruitment costs and logistical complexity. A smaller, more homogenous control group reduces costs but may limit the ability to detect subtle differences between parasomnia patients and healthy sleepers.
options: Recruit a large, demographically matched control group representing the general population to establish a broad baseline
Recruit a smaller, highly selective control group of individuals with no sleep complaints to maximize contrast with the parasomnia group
Employ a within-subject control design, comparing each participant's sleep patterns during periods with and without parasomnia events
characterized_levers.review: Control group size and composition directly impact the statistical power and generalizability of the study's findings.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Control group composition affects statistical power and generalizability, but is a methodological choice rather than a core strategic decision.
characterized_levers.description: This lever defines the characteristics of the control group, impacting the study's statistical power and generalizability. Key considerations include size, demographic matching, and the presence of sleep complaints. Success is measured by the ability to establish a robust baseline for comparison and minimize confounding variables, while managing recruitment costs.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Control Group Composition works in synergy with Participant Inclusion Criteria. Tighter inclusion criteria for the patient group necessitates a more carefully matched control group to avoid confounding.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Control Group Composition trades off against Recruitment Channel Mix. A larger, more diverse control group requires a broader and potentially more expensive recruitment strategy.

characterized_levers.name: Inter-Rater Reliability Threshold
characterized_levers.consequences: A higher inter-rater reliability threshold ensures greater accuracy and consistency in event scoring, but it also increases the time and effort required for adjudication and may lead to the exclusion of ambiguous events. A lower threshold reduces adjudication burden but increases the risk of misclassifying events and introducing bias into the analysis.
options: Require perfect agreement between raters for all events to ensure maximum accuracy and minimize subjective bias
Accept a moderate level of disagreement between raters, focusing on resolving discrepancies for only the most clinically significant events
Implement a tiered reliability system, requiring higher agreement for primary outcome measures and lower agreement for exploratory analyses
characterized_levers.review: The stringency of inter-rater reliability directly affects the accuracy and reproducibility of the study's findings.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Inter-rater reliability threshold affects data accuracy and reproducibility, but is a methodological detail rather than a core strategic decision.
characterized_levers.description: This lever sets the standard for agreement between raters scoring parasomnia events, directly influencing data accuracy and reproducibility. A higher threshold improves data quality but increases adjudication time and may exclude ambiguous events. Success is measured by achieving a balance between reliability and annotation throughput.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Inter-Rater Reliability Threshold amplifies the value of Annotation Granularity. Highly granular annotation requires higher inter-rater reliability to ensure consistency and validity of the detailed data.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Inter-Rater Reliability Threshold conflicts with Event-Triage Automation Level. Higher reliability standards may be harder to achieve when using automated triage tools, potentially requiring more manual review.

characterized_levers.name: Physiological Monitoring Density
characterized_levers.consequences: Increasing the density of physiological sensors (e.g., more EEG channels, additional EMG leads) enhances data richness and potentially improves event detection accuracy. However, it also increases participant burden, technician workload during setup and annotation, and data storage/processing demands. A higher density may also suppress naturalistic behavior if participants feel overly monitored.
options: Implement a minimalist sensor suite focused on core diagnostic signals to maximize participant comfort and minimize data processing overhead
Employ a high-density sensor array on all participants to capture subtle physiological changes associated with parasomnia events, accepting increased burden
Use an adaptive sensor array, starting with a minimalist set and escalating to higher density based on individual participant event frequency and data quality
characterized_levers.review: A minimalist sensor suite reduces participant burden, but may miss subtle physiological markers, while a high-density array increases data complexity and participant discomfort.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Physiological monitoring density impacts data richness and participant burden, but is a tactical decision within the data acquisition strategy.
characterized_levers.description: This lever determines the number and type of physiological sensors used during monitoring, impacting data richness and participant comfort. A higher density enhances event detection but increases participant burden and data processing demands. Success is measured by optimizing data quality while minimizing disruption to naturalistic sleep behavior.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Physiological Monitoring Density synergizes with Longitudinal Phenotyping Depth. Richer physiological data enables more detailed characterization of parasomnia events over time.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Physiological Monitoring Density conflicts with Residential Ambiance Design. A high-density sensor array can make the environment feel more clinical, potentially suppressing naturalistic behavior.

characterized_levers.name: Stay-Extension Protocol
characterized_levers.consequences: The criteria for extending participant stays directly influence event capture rates and overall study duration. More lenient extension criteria increase the likelihood of capturing events in low-frequency participants but also increase costs and potentially introduce selection bias. Stricter criteria reduce costs but may lead to underrepresentation of certain parasomnia subtypes.
options: Limit all participant stays to the initial 2–8 week period regardless of event capture to control costs and standardize data collection
Offer stay extensions to all participants with zero captured events to maximize the likelihood of capturing at least one event per participant
Offer stay extensions selectively based on a risk-benefit assessment considering participant characteristics, event history, and resource availability
characterized_levers.review: Limiting stays controls costs but risks missing events, while extending all stays maximizes capture but increases costs and potential selection bias.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: The stay-extension protocol influences event capture rates and study duration, but is a procedural matter rather than a core strategic choice.
characterized_levers.description: This lever defines the rules for extending participant stays, influencing event capture rates and study costs. More lenient criteria increase the likelihood of capturing events but also increase expenses and potential bias. Success is measured by maximizing event capture within budgetary constraints and minimizing selection bias.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Stay-Extension Protocol works with Participant Inclusion Criteria. Broader inclusion criteria may necessitate a more flexible stay-extension protocol to capture sufficient events.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Stay-Extension Protocol trades off against Unproductive Admission Handling. A more generous stay-extension policy may reduce the need to actively manage unproductive admissions, but increases costs.

characterized_levers.name: Annotation Granularity
characterized_levers.consequences: The level of detail in event annotation affects the richness of the longitudinal phenotyping data. Highly granular annotation captures subtle event characteristics but increases annotation time and requires more highly trained raters. Coarser annotation reduces annotation burden but may obscure important phenotypic variations.
options: Employ a coarse-grained annotation scheme focused on basic event classification to minimize annotation time and rater training requirements
Implement a highly granular annotation scheme capturing detailed event morphology, duration, and associated physiological changes to maximize phenotyping resolution
Use a tiered annotation scheme, starting with coarse-grained annotation and escalating to higher granularity for a subset of events based on research priorities
characterized_levers.review: Coarse annotation is faster but obscures detail, while granular annotation is richer but more time-consuming; tiered annotation balances depth and efficiency.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Annotation granularity affects the richness of the phenotyping data, but is a tactical decision within the data analysis strategy.
characterized_levers.description: This lever determines the level of detail captured during event annotation, impacting the richness of phenotyping data. Highly granular annotation captures subtle characteristics but increases annotation time and rater training. Success is measured by balancing annotation depth with annotation efficiency and rater expertise.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Annotation Granularity enhances Longitudinal Phenotyping Depth. More detailed annotation allows for a more nuanced and comprehensive characterization of parasomnia events over time.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Annotation Granularity conflicts with Event-Triage Automation Level. Highly granular annotation may be more difficult to automate, requiring more manual review and potentially limiting the effectiveness of triage tools.

characterized_levers.name: Data Security Protocol
characterized_levers.consequences: The stringency of data security measures impacts participant privacy and the risk of data breaches. More stringent measures (e.g., multi-factor authentication, air-gapped networks) increase security but also add complexity and cost. Less stringent measures reduce overhead but increase the risk of unauthorized access and data compromise.
options: Implement basic data security measures focused on compliance with university policies to minimize overhead and complexity
Employ state-of-the-art data security protocols including multi-factor authentication, encryption, and regular security audits to maximize data protection
Adopt a risk-based approach, tailoring security measures to the sensitivity of the data and the potential impact of a breach, balancing security and cost
characterized_levers.review: Basic security minimizes overhead but increases risk, while state-of-the-art protocols maximize protection but add complexity and cost.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Data security protocol impacts participant privacy and data breach risk, but is primarily a compliance and risk management issue, not a core strategic decision.
characterized_levers.description: The Data Security Protocol lever defines the measures taken to protect participant data, balancing security with cost and complexity. Key success metrics include compliance with regulations, prevention of data breaches, and efficient data access for research purposes. The protocol must address storage, access, and transfer of sensitive physiological and video data.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: A strong Data Security Protocol enhances the viability of the Physiological Monitoring Density lever by ensuring the privacy of the collected data, encouraging participant trust and retention.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: A stringent Data Security Protocol may conflict with Annotation Granularity if overly restrictive access controls hinder the timely and detailed annotation of data by research staff.

characterized_levers.name: Unproductive Admission Handling
characterized_levers.consequences: The approach to handling unproductive participant admissions (i.e., those with zero captured events) affects resource allocation and recruitment strategy. Ignoring unproductive admissions can lead to wasted resources, while aggressively excluding them may introduce selection bias and limit sample diversity. A balanced approach is needed to optimize resource utilization and maintain representativeness.
options: Continue admitting participants based on the initial inclusion criteria regardless of the unproductive admission rate to maintain sample diversity
Implement stricter inclusion criteria and more rigorous pre-screening to minimize unproductive admissions, potentially sacrificing sample diversity
Conduct a periodic review of inclusion criteria and pre-screening procedures based on the unproductive admission rate, iteratively refining the recruitment strategy
characterized_levers.review: Ignoring unproductive admissions wastes resources, while aggressively excluding them risks bias; iterative refinement balances efficiency and representativeness.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: Unproductive admission handling affects resource allocation and recruitment strategy, but is a tactical decision within the overall recruitment process.
characterized_levers.description: The Unproductive Admission Handling lever determines how the research team responds to participants who do not exhibit parasomnia events during their stay. It balances resource efficiency with the need to maintain a representative sample. Key metrics include the unproductive admission rate, recruitment costs, and sample diversity.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Effective Unproductive Admission Handling supports the Recruitment Channel Mix by informing which channels yield the most productive participants, allowing for resource optimization.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Stricter Unproductive Admission Handling may conflict with Participant Inclusion Criteria, potentially requiring adjustments to broaden the criteria and maintain enrollment targets.
